14_marg1035: BEDE. 'Anaglypha' in Greek are called 'celaturae', carvings, in Latin, because to the works of the virtues which the Church exercises throughout the world in holy and perfect men, those above all to whom the care of the faithful is committed and the keys of the kingdom of heaven given ought to apply themselves with all diligence, that as much as they are above the rest in rank so much they may excel in the merit of good action. For they have on themselves the figure of the cherubim carved when they imitate in mind and work, as far as they can, the angelic life on earth. They have figures of palm trees when they meditate with fixed intention on the heavenly retribution; for the palm is the adornment of the victor's hand. They have carvings very much projecting when they show to all most certain proofs of good works, which no one can interpret amiss. And all these are covered with golden plates when, beyond the other flowers of the virtues, the brightness of love shines preeminent in the great members of the Church. To these little doors a veil was added, as is written in Paralipomenon: "He made also a veil," it says, "of violet, purple, scarlet, and silk: and wrought cherubims in it." For the sake of beauty, namely, that among the gilded walls silk too might shine, but in the same signification as the little doors. It was hung before the ark and the entrance of the oracle, that, as the little doors were opened at fitting hours, so the veil too might be drawn back for those coming who entered into the holy of holies. The careful drawing back of this veil, then, signifies the opening of the law and of the heavenly kingdom which was given us through the incarnation of Christ. Whence when the Lord was baptized the heavens were opened, to show that through the baptism which he consecrated for us we must enter the gate of heaven; and when he died on the cross likewise "the veil was rent in the midst from the top even to the bottom," showing that the figures of the law were now ended, and the truth of the gospel and the heavenly secrets, and the very entrance of heaven, were no longer to be prophesied and signified figuratively, but to be opened at once to all who from the beginning of the world up to that time had passed from the world in the faith of truth. For on the fortieth day after the Lord's resurrection all sought heaven with him, and, every veil removed, received many mansions in the Father's house according to their merits. For us too, who were yet to be, the entrance was unbarred in that same hour, but only through inward desires of inward goods, through faith and the sacraments of the Lord's passion, through the fervour of sincere love, through the mortification of the concupiscence of the flesh, and through the daily help of the angels. Whence that same veil, under which one entered into the oracle, was made of violet, purple, scarlet and silk, and cherubims were woven into it. For violet, which imitates the colour of the sky, is compared to the desires of heavenly things. Purple, which is made from the blood of shellfish and displays a bloody hue, signifies the sacrament of the Lord's passion, which we must imitate by carrying our cross. In the scarlet of red colour is expressed the virtue of love, of which it is said: "Was not our heart burning within us" of Jesus "whilst he spoke to us in the way" etc. Silk, which springs green from the earth and by the long labour of craftsmen puts off its native greenness and is brought to whiteness, suggests the chastisement of the flesh, whose inborn moisture, as it were, the Apostle bids to be dried up, saying: "Mortify therefore your members which are upon the earth; fornication, uncleanness" etc. And to what grace of whiteness he would have it brought he shows elsewhere, saying: "I beseech you that you present your bodies a living sacrifice, holy, pleasing unto God" etc. Cherubims are woven in and made with the same colours when, in all that we do piously, we are protected by the Lord's gift from the poisoned darts of the demons through the guard of the angels. Cherubims are woven in when, in the good things we do, we use the multitude of knowledge unceasingly, looking always to the divine words, and, lest perhaps we stray from the path of the virtues, rule our steps continually by beholding them.
14_marg1036: As the entrance of the oracle, by which one came to the ark of the Lord and the cherubims, signifies 'the entrance of heaven', by which we desire to be brought to the vision of God and of the heavenly citizens, so the entrance into the temple [signifies] the beginnings of our conversion to God, when we enter into the present Church. This designates our entrance to faith, that one to hope. Whence the posts of this entrance are foursquare, on account of the four books of the gospel, by whose teaching we are instructed in the faith of truth.
14_marg1037: BEDE. Foursquare, namely on account of the four principal virtues: prudence, fortitude, justice, temperance, on which, as on a most firm foundation, the whole structure of good acts rests. For prudence is that by which we learn what we should do and how it befits us to live. Fortitude, that by which we fulfil what we have learned is to be done; these the prophet briefly embraces, saying: "The Lord is my light and my salvation, whom shall I fear?" Light, namely, that he may teach what we ought to do; salvation, that he may strengthen us to do it. Temperance is that by which we discern, lest we give ourselves more or less than is just to prudence and fortitude. And because whoever uses prudence, fortitude and temperance is truly just, justice follows fourth after prudence, fortitude and temperance.
14_interl1398: the love of God and of neighbour
14_marg1038: Because they look toward one another, so that the one cannot be had without the other: the outer door is brotherly love, the inner divine, because the former is first in time, the latter higher in dignity, and through the former one enters the latter; for in the love of neighbour one learns how the creator ought to be loved.
14_marg1039: BEDE. Because in each love two things are chiefly to be observed. In the love of God, the faith of truth and purity of working: "For without faith it is impossible to please God," and: "Faith without works is dead." In the love of brotherhood, patience and kindness. Whence: "Charity is patient, is kind," that is, that it may forgive the injuries of neighbours and do good to them. Whence: "Forgive, and you shall be forgiven. Give, and it shall be given to you." This love we desire to be spent on us, saying: "Give us this day our daily bread, and forgive us our debts, as we also forgive our debtors."
14_marg1040: Each door was opened holding one another, because the virtues are joined and cannot be separated; for neither faith without works nor works without faith please, nor does it suffice to bear injuries for one who does not impart necessaries to him whom he bears with, nor to supply necessaries for one who does not know how to forgive from the heart the troubles brought upon him. For the opening of the doors does not signify a separation of the virtues, but that through their joining the entrance of the Church lies open to us more and more, that the more we abound in them the more truly we may be joined to the companies of the saints; just as the dividing of the Red Sea, by which the people of God escaped the pursuing Egyptian, signified not a division of baptism but an opening, by which, all sins being extinguished, we pass over to the shore and firm ground of the virtues.
14_marg1041: BEDE. It is to be noted that in the entrance of the oracle there are said to have been two doors, but not double; but in the entrance of the temple, that is, of the former house, there were two doors such that each was double, because in the present Church it is needful for us to enter and lead such a life that we keep the love of God and neighbour through faith and working, through patience and kindness. But in the future life, where we shall see God and our neighbours in the light of eternal beatitude, we shall enjoy the same twofold love without labour but in the highest sweetness. Whence the entrance of the inner house had two doors, but single. For faith is not necessary there, where we shall see openly what we now believe and hope; nor the labour of works, because we shall be given the perpetual wage of what we labour at here; nor patience, where there is nothing adverse; nor the bounty of kindness, where there is no need.
14_marg1042: According to the form of the work it was provided, for the sake of beauty, that in the same entrance of the temple there should be two doors. For it was necessary that the walls of the house, which had a hundred and twenty cubits in height, should also have some cubits of thickness; at the outer edge of this thickness the doors were fixed, so that each door was level with the wall, and whether one stood within or without the temple and looked at the door, it should seem to him in every way one wall. Likewise the cedar wall, since it was twenty cubits in length and height, had no small thickness. Therefore in its entrance too two doors were made, that on each side, that is, within and without, the door might show level with the wall. And since the door and the wall had the same figures, so that it might seem one wall stretched out in every way and continuously, the one displaying [the grace] of beauty, the other prefiguring the dispensation of a mystery.
14_marg1043: Or the door which held together is opened when by the ministry of the preacher it is discerned what properly belongs to the knowledge of faith and what to chastity of living, which two cannot be separated; and that it is little to bear the evils of neighbours and not to bestow good things on them, since these are most surely wont to abide indissolubly in the hearts of the perfect.
14_marg1044: These things have been explained above, because on the walls of the house and on the inner doors the same figures or carvings were made, because the same mysteries of faith, hope and charity which the lofty and perfect grasp loftily, and which all the elect perceive fully in the eternal vision, are also handed on to the rude who are to be catechized, to be learned and confessed according to each one's capacity, that, initiated into the sacred mysteries, they may at length come to grasp what they have believed.
14_marg1045: AND HE BUILT THE INNER COURT etc. BEDE. Of the inner court he speaks briefly; of the outer he seems to be altogether silent; but in the Words of the Days [Paralipomenon] mention is made of both, where it is written: "He made also the court of the priests, and a great hall, and doors in the hall, which he covered with brass." Now the inner court, which is called the priests' because the priests and Levites ministered in it, surrounded the temple on every side; but on the east, whence was the entrance of the temple, it was set apart much farther from the temple than on the other three sides, because on that side, that is, before the face of the temple, the ministries of the holy things were done. There was the brazen altar for offering victims to the Lord, there the ten lavers for washing them, there the brazen sea was placed for washing the hands and feet of the priests when they went in to minister. And this court had three cubits of height, as Josephus relates, to keep the rest from the entrance of the temple and signify that this was lawful for the priests alone. And it had a gate on the eastern side, up to which the people brought their victims and sacrifices to be received by the priests and carried to the altar. Of the outer court, which the Words of the Days call the great hall, Josephus wrote thus: "Outside this temple he built another hall made in a four-cornered figure, raising very great and broad porches and setting in it high and ample gates toward the four parts of the world, each of which faced toward its own wind at the four corners, where he placed golden doors." And a little after: "Into this sanctuary, then, all the people entered in whom was purification and the observance of the legal ordinances." These porches Cassiodorus, in the picture of the temple which he set on a wall, as he mentions in the exposition of the psalms, distinguished in a threefold order: setting the first order outside the court of the priests on every side in a square; the second in the same way outside the inmost porches, turned round about on every side; the outermost likewise on every side around the former porches. And so the temple was fortified on every side by a threefold defence of buildings, a pavement of marble being made under the open sky between the several buildings, and the inner walls of the houses, that is, those which looked toward the temple, being made solid on the outer columns. And so it came about that the whole structure of the temple was reasonably distinguished by variety of degrees. For the high priest entered into the holy of holies; into the temple itself the priests, [unclear in the edition: "purificari et non purificati"], together with the Levites and singers; into the inmost court of the greater hall the purified Jewish men, standing and praying under the open sky if it was fair, and if stormy betaking themselves into the nearest porches; into the outer court the purified Jewish women; into the outermost court the gentiles, and Jews who had lately come from the gentiles, up to the sixth day of purification. These things, as we found them distinguished in the picture of Cassiodorus, we have briefly noted, judging that he learned them from the ancient Jews, and that so learned a man would not have wished to set forth as an example for readers what he had not first known to be true. These places are recalled by the psalm of the last of the gradual psalms, which begins thus: "Behold now bless ye the Lord, all ye servants of the Lord: who stand in the house of the Lord, in the courts of the house of our God." In these porches Jeremias and the other prophets, in these the Lord and the apostles preached. In one of these the Lord was sitting teaching when, the Pharisees tempting him, the woman was brought to him [unclear in the edition: "ad vitam iudicanda"]. In these he found those selling sheep and oxen and doves, whom he cast out of the temple. In these Peter and John, finding the lame man, healed him and, going in with him, led him further in to pray. In these the whole multitude of the people was praying when the angel appeared to Zachary as he offered incense at the altar of incense and taught him fully of the birth of the Lord's forerunner.
14_marg1046: But these courts with their porches could not hide the sight of the temple from those looking at it from afar, because the place in which the temple was was much higher than where the porches were. For as Josephus wrote: "The outermost structures of the courts, though raised to four hundred cubits, yet did not reach to the top of the mount on which the temple was built." These things about the structure of the temple we have thought should be made known to the studious reader. But in those things which sacred Scripture thought fit to relate let us seek the figures of mysteries; the rest let us use simply for knowledge of the history.
14_marg1047: The building of the temple within the court of the priests, then, expresses the life of the perfect in the Church, who by excellence of virtues draw near to the Lord and show to others the guidance of salvation by word and work. For a priest, sacerdos, is so called because he affords sacred guidance, sacrum ducatum, to the lesser; by which name are counted not only the ministers of the altar, namely bishops and presbyters, but also all who excel in loftiness of doctrine and conversation and profit not themselves only but many, who, while they present "their bodies a living sacrifice, holy, pleasing unto God," spiritually exercise the priestly ministry. Whence Peter says to the whole Church: "But you are a chosen generation, a kingly priesthood, a holy nation, a purchased people." And to the ancient people it is said: "You shall be to me a priestly kingdom, and a holy nation."
14_marg1048: But the great hall which was outside the court of the priests, in which all the people were wont to pray or hear the word, figures the life and manners of the carnal in the Church, to whom the Apostle says: "I could not speak to you as unto spiritual, but as unto carnal" etc. These are well signified by the great hall, because the number of such in the Church is much greater than that of the perfect. But as much as they surpass in number, so much they fall short in merit. Whence this hall holds very many, yet does not admit them into the inner parts of the gilded temple, nor to the office of the altar, nor into the court of the priests itself; because the carnal and the weak, though for the merit of chaste faith and piety they belong to the lot of the elect, are yet far from being made equal to those who say with confidence: "I dare not to speak of any of those things which Christ worketh not by me, for the obedience of the Gentiles, by word and deed," and: "I have fought a good fight" etc.
14_marg1049: The common people came up to the court of the priests and brought their victims to the gate, and followed with their eyes the victims received by the priests and offered on the altar. Into the temple itself too, when it was opened, they looked from afar, and yet could not enter even the court of the priests. But from the lower places they cried to the Lord, because the simplicity of the carnal in the Church is not despised by the Lord when they faithfully offer what vows of piety they can. For they look from afar into the temple of the Lord when they rejoice to learn and admire the life of the lofty, and embrace with the affection of devout veneration those whom they cannot follow by imitation of virtue. They see the victims of the priests consumed on the altar by the sacred fire, because they know that the great works of the great are graciously accepted by the Lord through the Spirit.
14_marg1050: They bring their victims to the court of the priests, to be offered to the Lord through them, when, doing what good they can, they are strengthened by the exhortation of their elders and the more learned and commended by their intercession. They also offer victims to the priests, commending them to the Lord through them, when they give the needy saints the necessaries in which they abound, with a view to the reward. Whence: "Amen I say to you, he shall not lose his reward." And so the same fire consumes the victims of both on the altar of God, when the Lord judges the alms of the rich, together with the great virtues of the saints, worthy of his regard and recompense. The multitude of believers, then, who, having left their possessions, served God with one heart and one soul, is itself the temple of God and the place within the court of the priests specially consecrated to him. But the great hall, and those praying in it round about the court of the priests, figure those who in their time believed from among the gentiles in Syria and in Antioch and the other provinces and cities, on whom the apostles and elders who were at Jerusalem laid no more burden than that they abstain "from things sacrificed to idols, and from blood, and from things strangled, and from fornication." By whose offerings, however, they wished the poor among the saints who were at Jerusalem to be supported, that, ministering carnal things to them, they might become partakers of their spiritual things. But Barnabas and Paul with their companions, who received their offerings and carried them to Jerusalem, are the priests who, receiving the victims, bring them to the altar of the Lord to be consecrated, because they brought the gifts of their devotion to the saints, who would pray for them. The court, then, set between the place of the people and of the priests, signifies that division which sets apart the carnal in the Church, and those lately beginning, from the citadel of the perfect, not by the lot of election but by the measure of merits. For the carnal believe it suffices them if they have faith, hope and charity and purity of works. The perfect, over and above all these, labour in preaching the word, give all they have to the poor, give themselves to vigils, fasts, hymns, spiritual canticles and sacred discourses, bear persecutions and dangers for justice' sake, and carry out with ready devotion of mind the other things which Paul glories that he did. Whence it follows: HE BUILT THE INNER COURT WITH THREE ROWS OF STONES etc.
14_interl1400: because a sure diligence in learning is necessary, that each may discern what he ought to believe, what to hope, or what to love
14_interl1401: namely by good working without the corruption of pretence, without the addition of which faith, hope and charity cannot be true
14_marg1051: The one row of cedar beams is good working, shown without the corruption of pretence, without the addition of which faith, hope and charity cannot be true. For cedar wood, on account of the grace of its fragrance and the incorruptible power of its nature, designates the perseverance and good fame of devout action. Up to this court all the elect ascend who seek to please God by faith, hope, charity and work. This the perfect pass beyond by the lofty grace of merits when they advance to such a height of virtues that they can say to their hearers: "Be ye followers of me, as I also am of Christ," and: "Know you not that we shall judge angels? how much more things of this world?"
14_marg1052: BEDE. It is asked how the house of the Lord is said to have been finished in the eighth month in all its work and in all its vessels, when in what follows it is read that its dedication was completed in the seventh month. Nor is it credible that Solomon, building the temple for seven years, finished it in the eighth month of the eighth year, or put off the dedication of the finished [house] to the seventh month of the ninth year. Whence it seems rather likely that the house was built in seven years and seven months, so that the dedication was celebrated in that same seventh month, and on the twenty-third day of that month, according to Paralipomenon, Solomon sent the people away to their tents; and so, after one week, when the eighth month came, the house of the Lord was finished, namely all its works, the dedication itself having been completed before. Unless perhaps it is to be thought that after the temple was dedicated some vessels were added for its ministries up to the beginning of the eighth month, the king hastening so as to dedicate the temple wholly in the seventh month, which was all solemn; and so both are found true: that the temple was finished in the eighth month in all its work and vessels, and that it was dedicated in the seventh month.
14_marg1053: But that the house was finished in all its work in the eighth year and its eighth month pertains to the world to come and the day of judgment, when the Church shall come to such perfection that nothing can be found to be added to it. For then Christ will show us the Father, and it will suffice us. Now the day of judgment is expressed typically by the number eight, because it follows this world, which runs in seven days. Whence David entitled a psalm 'for the octave', which he sang for fear of the judgment, saying: "O Lord, rebuke me not in thy indignation, nor chastise me in thy wrath."
14_marg1054: Because the Church is built of elect souls through the whole time of this world, which is run through in the circuit of seven days, and at the end of the world brings its growth to an end. Or for the signification of spiritual grace, through which alone the Church receives [the power] to be the Church; because without the gifts of the Spirit no one can be made faithful, or keep the faith, or by the merit of faith come to the crown of justice.

14_marg1058: BEDE. The column before the doors of the temple is eighteen cubits high when the preacher openly suggests to all that only through faith and the works of justice can we come to the joys of the life above. The name of Jesus too among the Greeks begins from this number. For the first letter of this name signifies ten, the second eight. And fittingly the columns of the house of God are eighteen cubits high, because the holy teachers tend by living well to this, that they may deserve to see their creator face to face; for nothing further is to be sought when they have come to him who is above all.
14_marg1059: Of whom Paul [says]: "James and Cephas and John, who seemed to be pillars" etc. By which words he seems to expound the mystery of the material columns, namely both what they figured and why they are two. For they signify the apostles and all teachers, strong in faith and work and upright in contemplation. And they are two, that by preaching they may bring the foreskin and the circumcision into the Church. They stood in the porch before the doors of the temple and adorned its entrance with their beauty on either side. Now the door of the temple is the Lord, who says: "No man cometh to the Father, but by me." And elsewhere: "I am the door" etc. This door the columns set on each side surround when the ministers of the word show the entrance of heaven to both peoples, so that whether one comes to the faith of the gospel from the light of legal knowledge or from the rigour of heathenism, he may have them ready to minister to him the way of salvation by word and example. Or because of these columns it is written in Paralipomenon: "These pillars he set up in the porch of the temple, one on the right hand, and the other on the left," therefore two columns were made, and so placed that they teach us to keep the entrance of the heavenly homeland before the eyes of the mind in prosperity and in adversity. Paul, a column of the house of the Lord, exhorts us by his own and his followers' examples to be armed "by the armour of justice on the right hand and on the left," that, neither delighted by prosperity nor broken by hardships, we may in no part turn aside from the right way by which we go to the promised homeland.
14_marg1060: For three times six makes eighteen. Three, namely, pertains to faith on account of the Trinity, but six to working, because the world was made in six days. Three is multiplied by six when "the just man liveth by faith" and heaps up the knowledge of devout faith with the carrying out of good action.
14_marg1061: BEDE. The rule of apostolic institution compasses each column when the teacher, sent to preach to Jews or gentiles, takes care to do and teach only those things which the Church received and learned through the apostles. For he who will teach, live or preach otherwise, and spurns the apostolic decrees, or establishes new things at his own pleasure, is not a column in the temple of God, because while he scorns to follow the apostolic institutions, whether by the thinness of sloth or the thickness of pride, he does not agree with the line of twelve cubits.
14_interl1412: four, therefore, in diameter, since it was twelve cubits round
14_marg1062: HE MADE ALSO TWO CHAPITERS etc. BEDE. The heads of the columns, that is, their highest part, are the hearts of the teachers, by whose thoughts devoted to God, as the members by the head, so their works and words are directed. And the two chapiters set on the heads are the two testaments, to the meditation and observance of which teachers are subject in mind and body. Whence each chapiter has five cubits of height, because the Scripture of the Mosaic law is comprised in five books, and the whole course of the old Testament embraced five ages of the world. But the New Testament preaches nothing other than what Moses and the prophets foretold by their preaching. Whence: "For if you did believe Moses, you would perhaps believe me also." Since, then, by a wonderful concord of the divine working the grace of the New Testament was hidden in the veil of the Old, and now the sacraments of the Old are revealed through the light of the New, each chapiter of the column is as it were five cubits high, because it is manifest that the grace of gospel perfection is implanted in the Old, whose sacraments are more fully comprised in five ages.
14_marg1063: This is written thus in Paralipomenon: "He made also as it were little chains in the oracle, and he put them on the tops of the pillars." For the appearance of chains and the likeness of a net on the chapiters is the variety of special virtues in the saints. Whence: "The queen stood on thy right hand, in gilded clothing," that is, in the clothing of shining love, "surrounded with variety" of divers gifts. Or the manifold weaving of the chains and the spreading of the net suggests the many kinds of persons among the elect who, while they cling by faithfully obeying the words of the preachers, set as it were on the heads of the columns, offer to all beholders the marvel of their linking as nets and little chains. For these chains are woven together with one another with wonderful work, because it was done by the wonderful grace of the Spirit that the life of the faithful, much separated by places, times, rank, condition, sex and age, is joined by one faith and love.
14_marg1064: Whence: "Which are the seven Spirits of God, sent forth into all the earth." Which Isaias explains more plainly, saying: "And the spirit of the Lord shall rest upon him: the spirit of wisdom, and of understanding, the spirit of counsel, and of fortitude" etc. There were seven rows of nets on each chapiter, because the fathers of both Testaments received that they should be elect through the grace of the one sevenfold Spirit.
14_marg1065: BEDE. It seems that the pomegranates were made round about the chapiters on the lower part, and from these pomegranates arose the nets by which the chapiters were covered in some part; it is signified that virtues are born of virtues, and that the saints go from virtue to virtue.
14_marg1066: BEDE. There were two rows of nets round the chapiter, but each row ran in a sevenfold order of lines until, the chapiter being gone round, it returned into itself as if a circle were made; namely because we are commanded to love God with the whole heart and our neighbour as ourselves, but each row has seven rows of nets, because neither God nor neighbour is loved without spiritual grace. For it is said by a truthful sentence: "The charity of God is poured forth in our hearts by the Holy Ghost." And likewise [that] of neighbour, because the one cannot be without the other. These nets were made to cover the chapiters, that is, to surround them on every side round about, because all holy Scripture, when rightly understood, sounds throughout the grace of charity and peace. For the chapiters are the divine volumes, the nets the bonds of mutual love. And the chapiters are covered with nets when the sacred words are proved to be clothed on every side with the gift of charity. For in those things also which we do not understand in the Scriptures charity lies hidden, and in those we understand it lies widely open.
14_marg1067: BEDE. Since it is said of the nets that they covered the chapiters which were upon the top of the pomegranates, it seems, according to the order of the work itself, that the pomegranates were made round about the chapiters on the lower part, and from those pomegranates arose the nets by which the chapiters were in some part covered. And the mystery is plain why the nets were joined over the top of the pomegranates, which pertain almost to one signification, of persons or of virtues. For we know that virtues are born of virtues, and that the saints go from virtue to virtue until the God of gods be seen in Sion, than which no greater virtue can be reached. Whence: "Tribulation worketh patience; and patience trial; and trial hope." In the very company of the elect too the persons of the just succeed one another, and the lesser rejoice to cleave to the footsteps of their forerunners, defended by their sayings or writings lest they fall into error. The nets, then, are set over the top of the pomegranates when the heart of charity is added over perfect works, and the life of the saints shines by both paths of virtue, namely by working and by charity, as if the linking of the nets were joined, added on above, to the circle of pomegranates on the chapiters of the column. And since all the present gifts of the virtues look to the eternal reward which is promised and ministered to us through the gospel, it is fitly added: and the chapiters that were upon the top of the pillars etc.
14_marg1068: Which, with one rind outside, surround many grains within, as the Church with one defence of faith encloses innumerable hosts of the elect. The life and manners of each just man too can be signified, who, as if embracing very many grains with one rind, hedges in the many signs of thoughts and virtues with the firm guard of faith and humility, lest they fall away. And well were the heads of the columns surrounded round about with pomegranates, because the holy teachers call to mind the life of the former faithful and by their examples defend their own acts and words on every side, lest, if they live otherwise, they go astray. As, then, the linking of the nets signifies the unity of the faithful in the bond of peace, so the pomegranates suggest that same unity which holds countless peoples together by one rule of faith. Or the linking of the nets shows the manifest concord of the faithful; but the placing of the pomegranates the inward virtues of the mind which cannot be seen by others, namely patience, humility, kindness etc. And the outward appearance of the fruits appears as it were most beautiful, but the abundance of grains shut within does not appear, when the working of the saints is shown openly, but the grace of faith, hope and love and the other goods of the mind which is within is not seen.
14_marg1069: BEDE. By the lilies is designated the brightness of the homeland above and the pleasantness of paradise fragrant with the flowers of immortality; by the four cubits the gospel word, which promises the entrance of eternal beatitude and shows the way of arriving. When, then, the holy teachers show the lights of the heavenly kingdom promised to us in the four books of the gospel, they display, as the heads of the columns, the lily work of four cubits in themselves. Where it is to be noted, according to the letter, that when the lily work on the chapiters is said to be of four cubits, and it is not added whether of breadth or of height, it is left to the reader's judgment whether it ought to be understood in height or in breadth. But it is certain that the column which the cord of twelve cubits compassed had four cubits in thickness. For every circle has three times round as much space as it has in diameter. But whether we take breadth or height, the figure is clear, because only through the gospel did that longed-for voice sound to the world: "Do penance: for the kingdom of heaven is at hand."
14_marg1070: It is to be noted in this sentence of Paralipomenon that the same porch of the temple is also called the vestibule of the temple. Whence: "Between the porch and the altar [the priests] shall weep," that is, between the porch and the altar.
14_interl1413: of as great breadth as was this column; yet how great was the height of its chapiter is not said
14_marg1071: AND AGAIN OTHER CHAPITERS etc. BEDE. Whose making designates the loftiness of the everlasting kingdom which "eye hath not seen, nor ear heard, neither hath it entered into the heart of man" etc. For after the lilies of four cubits other chapiters were set, how great whose height was is not said, because we read many things of the heavenly beatitude in the gospel: namely that there the clean of heart shall see God, that they shall be equal to the angels of God, that they shall neither marry nor be married, because they can die no more, because 'where Christ is, there also shall his ministers be' etc., of this kind. But the very appearance of these things we have spoken of, the very state of the conversation of the heavenly homeland, how it is, lies open only to its citizens who have deserved to enter. Whence by the making or height of these chapiters which were above the lily is suggested the quality of the heavenly dwelling, incomprehensible to earthly beings. Of which, however, this is not hidden: that all there enjoy the common felicity of the divine vision, each the more loftily the cleaner eyes of the heart he has had for seeing. Common, then, is the blessing of all the elect there; but that the many mansions of the blessed in the one house of God are distinct according to the quality of works is signified when it is said: AND AGAIN OTHER CHAPITERS etc. The chapiters above are made according to the measure of the column when the holy teachers, indeed all the just following the footsteps of the teachers, receive the rewards of eternal retribution according to the merits of their working. The same chapiters are made above the nets too, because according to the measure of the love by which holy brotherhood is bound together in this life it will also be joined to the fellowship of the heavenly citizens in the presence of its creator. But because that fellowship is granted to the faithful of both peoples, it is rightly added: of pomegranates etc.
14_marg1072: By the pomegranate is signified the whole Church, but by the hundred, which is the first to pass to the right hand, eternal beatitude. This number of pomegranates is doubled round about the second chapiter, to signify that the people of both testaments is to be united in Christ and brought into the eternal crown. Whence: "For they were not far from the land, but as it were two hundred cubits, dragging the net with fishes." For over two hundred cubits the disciples drag the net full of great fishes to the Lord, who was already showing on the shore the effect of his resurrection, when the preachers commit the word of faith to Jews and gentiles and gather the elect of both peoples into one citadel of beatitude.
14_marg1073: THE PILLAR ON THE RIGHT HAND. The right column signifies 'the teachers of the primitive Church', the second 'those who were sent to preach to the gentiles'. Or the right signifies 'those who by prophesying foretold the Lord to come in the flesh', the second 'those who testify that he has now come and redeemed the world'. Both columns are reckoned by a like name. For one is called 'firmness', the other 'in strength', that one strength of faith and work might be shown to be in all teachers, and the sloth of our time silently noted, where certain teachers wish to be seen and called priests and columns of the house of God, when they have in themselves nothing of firm faith for despising the pomps of the world and desiring invisible goods, no strength for correcting, no diligence even for understanding, the errors of those over whom they are set.
14_marg1074: BEDE. This sea was made in figure of baptism, by which we are cleansed unto remission of sins. For the priests were washed in it, as Paralipomenon testifies. And all the elect are called priests, who are members of the high priest Jesus Christ. Rightly is this vessel called a sea, namely in memory of the Red Sea, in which formerly, through the destruction of the Egyptians and the deliverance of the people of God, the form of baptism went before. Whence: "Our fathers were all under the cloud, and all passed through the sea. And all in Moses were baptized, in the cloud, and in the sea." Now the sacrament of baptism both seeks of us cleanness of life in this world and promises the glory of eternal life in the future. Both of which are signified in the brazen sea when it is said to be ten cubits from brim to brim. For by ten precepts in the law the Lord expressed all that we ought to do; and by the denarius likewise he signified the wage of good deeds, when he foretold that it was to be given to those labouring in the vineyard.
14_interl1417: to signify that the whole world was to be cleansed from the filth of sins by the laver of life
14_marg1075: Because from the first baptized in the name of Jesus Christ to the last who is to believe and be baptized at the end of the world, the whole choir of the faithful must enter the same way of truth and hope from the Lord for a common crown of justice.
14_marg1076: Because whatever we sin by sight, hearing, taste, smell and touch, the grace of God remits to us through the washing of the life-giving font. But the remission of past sins does not suffice unless one thereafter apply himself to good works; otherwise the devil who had gone out of the man, if he sees him empty of good works, returns more manifold and makes the last state of that man worse than the first. Whence it is added: and a line of thirty cubits etc.
14_marg1077: The discipline of the heavenly precepts, by which we are bound back from pleasures. Whence "a threefold cord is not easily broken," because the observance of the commandments, which in the hearts of the elect is strengthened by faith, love and hope of the reward above, can be loosed by no obstacle. The line compasses the sea when we strive to fortify with devout works the sacrament of baptism which we have received. This is of thirty cubits; for five times six make thirty. And by six, in which the Lord made man when he was not and remade him when he had perished, our good working is figured. And six is multiplied by five to reach thirty when all the senses of the body are subjected to the divine commands.
14_marg1078: Otherwise. Three times ten make thirty, and the human race after the flood, from the progeny of the three sons of Noe, filled the breadth of the whole world. For the offspring of Sem held Asia, of Cham Africa, of Japheth Europe and the islands of the sea. And because the mystery of baptism, with the carrying out of works and the hope of heavenly things, was to be ministered to all nations, a line of thirty cubits girded the sea in which baptism was figured.
14_marg1079: But here too it is to be said that the Lord came to baptism when he was thirty years old; and since by his baptism, which he received at thirty, he consecrated our baptism, rightly did a cord of thirty cubits go round the sea which figured our baptism, to signify that by the gift of him who underwent baptism without sin, baptism is dedicated for us who believe in him unto the remission of sins.
14_marg1080: AND A GRAVEN WORK UNDER THE BRIM etc. Since it was said before that a line of thirty cubits went round the sea, and now it is added that this graven work placed under the brim compassed it for ten cubits, it is plain that the vessel was spread out and widened in the manner of a bowl, which was narrowed from the thirty cubits of compass which it had at the brim to ten. Now a storied carving is one which imitates some histories of things. Whence by the storied carvings with which the sea is surrounded are signified the examples of former times which we are to look upon, that we may see by what works the saints pleased God from the beginning, with what obstinacy the wicked persisted in their crimes, with what unhappiness the reprobate perished: how in the beginning of the newborn world Cain [so the edition: 'Cham'] was condemned for the malice of envy, Abel crowned for the merit of justice, Lamech cursed for adultery and homicide, Henoch brought back to paradise for the grace of piety; Cham after the flood abhorred for impiety, Sem and Japheth given an everlasting blessing for the service of reverence; Abraham made heir of the divine promise by the merit of faith, the rest of the multitude of nations left for unbelief. And when the Lord came in the flesh, Judea rejected for perfidy, the gentiles by grace brought back to salvation; and things of this kind, which, considered carefully in both testaments, profit the studious. Perhaps therefore there are two rows of storied carvings on the brazen sea, that those who have been steeped in the font of baptism may hearken to the histories of both testaments. Therefore they were ten cubits round about, that they may strive to imitate whomsoever they perceive in those same histories given to obeying the heavenly commands and suspended with their whole intention toward the rewards above.
14_marg1081: BEDE. [They signify] the apostles, the evangelists, indeed all ministers of the word. Whence: "Thou shalt not muzzle the ox that treadeth out the corn" etc. These carry the sea set upon them when the apostles and their successors fulfil with ready devotion the office of the gospel enjoined on them: OF WHICH THREE LOOKED TOWARDS THE NORTH etc., because in all the parts of the four-square world they preach the faith of the Trinity. Hence too twelve apostles, that is, four times three, were chosen, that, preaching the faith and confession of the Trinity through the four quarters of the world, they might baptize all nations in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Ghost. The words, acts and passions of them and their successors we can easily see and know at present by reading; but what glory of recompense awaits them in the future we cannot yet see.
14_interl1418: the firmness of virtue in baptism
14_interl1420: Paralipomenon [says] a handbreadth; Josephus four fingers
14_marg1082: BEDE. He who receives the laver of baptism unto salvation and life ought to have faith and hope and charity, without which no one can work rightly. Whence it is added: The thickness of the laver was three inches.
14_marg1083: BEDE. Because the reception of baptism is fortified by the strength of faith, hope and charity, and it is shown to be of no profit to the receivers otherwise, unless the firm certainty of these virtues strengthens the mind and bodies of the receivers.
14_interl1421: the taste of the Lord's passion
14_interl1422: "Father, if it be possible, let this chalice pass from me"
14_marg1084: BEDE. The lily, with the accompanying grace of fragrance, shows a white colour without and a golden one within; therefore it suggests the glory of the resurrection of him who showed outwardly to the disciples the immortality of his body, and taught that a soul shining with divine light was at the same time within him. Christ too before his passion was as it were a lily still closed, when he shone forth as a man renowned for miracles. But after the resurrection and ascension he showed himself a lily spread open to the birds of heaven, to whom in the humanity he had taken he showed the power of the divine "glory which he had before the world was." Whence: "I am the flower of the field, and the lily of the valleys." The brim of the sea, then, in which the priests are washed, was as it were the brim of a cup and the leaf of a crisped lily, because baptism, by which we are made members of the high priest, purifies us from sins in the faith of his passion, and brings the purified to the vision of his glory. In this laver the people of the circumcision and of the foreskin are made one in the Lord through faith, hope and love. Whence: "Other sheep I have" up to "and there shall be one fold and one shepherd." Whence it is added: it contained two thousand bates etc.
14_marg1085: BEDE. The bate is a measure of the Hebrews, which among them is called bath, having three modii; it is the same as the ephi, which they call epha. But the ephi pertains to the measure of grain, the bate to liquids, namely wine, water and oil. The bate, then, which is the standard of a fixed measure, signifies the works of equity and justice in which those who are baptized unto remission of sins must be instructed. The sea holds a thousand bates when the water of baptism, washing the people of the Jews, sends them on to the heavenly kingdom. It holds another thousand when it makes the gentiles, reborn in the same font and strengthened by works of justice, partakers of the same kingdom.
14_marg1086: BEDE. A thousand signifies perfection, because it makes the solid square of ten. For ten times ten make a hundred, which is a figure already square but still flat. But that it may rise in height and be made solid, multiply a hundred by ten and they make a thousand. By this number the stable and as it were square conscience of the just is signified. For whichever way you turn a square it will stand; so the mind of the elect is bent from the state of rectitude by no temptation.
14_interl1425: a bate holds a measure and a half
14_marg1087: AND HE MADE TEN BASES etc. In many ways and in divers manners the same sacraments of our salvation are figured. For the apostles and apostolic men, as they are signified by the oxen carrying the sea, so also by the bases which were made ready for carrying the lavers, just as the lavers themselves, like the sea, figured the spiritual laver. But indeed according to Paralipomenon they washed in them all things that they were to offer as holocaust. Now the holocaust of the Lord is understood generally as the whole multitude of the elect, which is baptized in the Holy Spirit and fire. As, then, the priests who were washed in the sea signify those who through baptism are made sharers of the high priest who is in Christ Jesus, so the holocausts too signify the same when through the washing of baptism they are filled with the grace of the Holy Spirit. For the victim is washed in the laver when the faithful one is bathed in baptism; it is offered as a holocaust when by the laying on of the bishop's hand he receives the gift of the Holy Spirit. Philip, when he preached in Samaria, was washing victims in the laver of the temple; but because the Spirit had not yet come down upon any of them, but they were only baptized in the name of the Lord Jesus, as washed victims they had not yet come to the fire of the altar. But when Peter and John, sent there, laid their hands on them, and receiving the Spirit they spoke with tongues, the victims had now come to the fire of the altar, to become a holocaust, that is, wholly burnt, because spiritual grace, filling their consciences, made them glow with divine love.
14_marg1088: BEDE. That ten bases were made for carrying the lavers could be interpreted mystically thus: that the ministers of baptism call those whom they instruct to the eternal joy which is figured in the denarius. But because it follows that five were placed on the right side of the temple, five on the left, rather the mystery of the number five is to be noted in them. For the bases of the lavers were placed on both sides of the temple, to signify that the grace of baptism was to be opened to both peoples. And there are five on each side, to signify that all that they had sinned through the five senses of the body was to be remitted to the faithful in baptism. As, then, in the one sea set upon the oxen is expressed the unity of baptism to be preached by the apostles through the whole world, so by the two rows of lavers [it is expressed] that the gentiles and Judea were to be gathered into one faith through baptism. For although the victims were washed in the twin lavers, some on the right, some on the left, they were yet consumed by the one fire of the altar to become a holocaust. For whoever, Jew or gentile, receives baptism, all are sanctified by one Spirit to become sons of God. Whence: "Whereby we cry: Abba, Father" etc.: in various tongues, namely, according to the diversity of nations, but calling on God the Father by one and the same name because of the gift of the one Spirit.
14_interl1426: there are four principal virtues on which the whole structure of the virtues rests
14_marg1089: BEDE. The length and breadth of the bases was of four cubits each, because the preachers, whether they bear outwardly the adversities of the world and the length of exile and of present labours, or enlarge the heart inwardly with exultation in the love of God and neighbour, always apply themselves to the virtues: namely discerning prudently between good and evil, bravely bearing adversities, tempering the heart from the desire of pleasures, holding to justice in working.
14_interl1430: because through the exercise of the virtues which they practise with patience toward the wicked and love of the good they always aspire to the vision of the holy Trinity
14_interl1431: of hope, namely of the reward above
14_interl1432: hollow within; whence: And gravings etc.
14_marg1090: AND THE WORK ITSELF etc. The tables of which the bases were made were square, and in them were round forms which are called little crowns or ledges, in the midst of which were carvings of lions etc.
14_interl1433: by which, namely, the tables of the lavers were bound to one another, so that of four or five tables one base was made; and what carvings the bases had between these joinings, that is, on their sides, before and behind, right and left, and also above, he reveals, saying: between the little crowns
14_marg1091: BETWEEN THE LITTLE CROWNS AND THE LEDGES etc. BEDE. The surface of the bases was flat in no part, but carved on every side with mystical figures, because the minds of the saints, indeed their whole conversation, displays the grace of the virtues; nor does any hour pass empty in which they are not occupied with devout works and words or thoughts. For they have little crowns carved on themselves when they pant with unwearied desire for the entrance of everlasting life; ledges, when amid the desires of the heavenly life which is above they do not loose the bonds of brotherly charity which is near at hand. They have lions between the little crowns and the ledges when they so lift up the mind to hope for heavenly things, and so enlarge it to love their neighbours, that they inveigh sharply against the sinners committed to them. They have oxen with the lions when they show the rebuke of correction with the spirit of meekness; when in the fervour of reproving they never cease to have the cloven hoof of discreet action and speech, never cease to turn over in the mouth, as by chewing the cud, the words of the divine reading. Stephen, an eminent base, showed the fierce teeth and claws of lions to his persecutors, saying: "You stiffnecked and uncircumcised in heart" etc.; but the meekness of the ox when he said: "Lord, lay not this sin to their charge." But since we can have neither the hope of eternal things in heaven, nor the love of neighbours on earth, nor the fervour of biting zeal, nor the gentleness of compassionate modesty, without the knowledge of the Scriptures, well after the crowns and ledges, after the lions and oxen, are cherubims said to have been carved, who signify Scripture: either because two cherubims were made on the propitiatory of the ark in figure of the two Testaments singing in concord of Christ, or because they are interpreted 'multitude of knowledge'. And the more studiously one has applied himself to divine Scripture, the more in all that he does or judges he fears the judgment of God, lest, punishing sinners too much or pardoning without discretion, he incur the wrath of the judge. For he that addeth knowledge addeth also labour; whence here too after the carvings of the cherubims it is well added: and under the lions and oxen etc.
14_interl1435: by which they might seem bound
14_marg1092: BEDE. The four books of the gospels, which, as a turning wheel runs most swiftly where it is led, at the Lord's bidding filled the whole world in a short time through the apostles; and as a wheel lifts the chariot set upon it from the earth and carries it where the driver directs, so they lift the minds of the elect from earthly things to heavenly and lead them to the advance of working or the mystery of preaching whither spiritual grace wills to help; for it is added that the wheels were such as are wont to be made in a chariot. And we read of the saints: "The chariot of God is attended by ten thousands; thousands of them that rejoice" etc. If, then, the bases of the lavers are the teachers who minister the laver of life, and the four wheels of the bases the four gospels, the axletrees of the wheels which bear the bases are the hearts of the teachers, which, assiduous in the gospel precepts, raise them from the lowest things, and as the axletrees, the wheels being put on, lift the base higher from the earth.
14_marg1093: BEDE. [The undersetters,] which, set before the wheels, prevented them from slipping off the axletrees, are the proclamations of the prophets, by which the gospel and apostolic Scripture is confirmed, lest it come into doubt for any reader. Whence: "We have the more firm prophetical word: whereunto you do well to attend" etc. Whence Mark too says: "The beginning of the gospel of Jesus Christ, the Son of God. As it is written in Isaias the prophet," and Matthew: "Now all this was done that the scriptures of the prophets might be fulfilled."
14_marg1094: BEDE. Because all prophetic Scripture agrees with itself, as composed by one Spirit. And there were four undersetters to every base, namely according to the number of the wheels; not that there are only four prophetic books, but that all that the prophets spoke bore witness to the four gospels, that by the agreement of both Testaments one faith and love of Christ might strengthen the hearts of us all.
14_interl1438: the brim of the sea [was] like a crisped lily; on the contrary the mouth of the laver was turned inward, a mouth of one cubit; the bottom was of a cubit and a half, and the belly is believed to have been of four cubits
14_interl1439: to teach that through baptism the way to heavenly things has been opened to us
14_interl1440: on account of the unity of confession and faith by which all are baptized in the confession of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Ghost: "One Lord, one faith, one baptism, one God and Father of all"
14_marg1095: BEDE. On account of perfection, namely of work, and the merit of contemplation. For the whole cubit in the laver is the perfection of good action which he had of whom it was said: "Hast thou considered my servant Job, that there is none like him in the earth?" But the other cubit is of the divine vision, which is given to the faithful in some part in this life. Whence the same Job says of the vanquished adversary: "With the hearing of the ear I have heard thee, but now my eye seeth thee." Therefore after the cubit of good working, which can be perfected in the saints in this life, there begins the cubit of heavenly contemplation, which is to be perfected in the elect in the future life. And the measure of a cubit and a half was not in the lavers only, but also in their wheels and bases. Whence it follows: the height of a wheel was a cubit and [a half] etc.; and a little after: in the top of the base there was a round compass of a cubit and a half etc. The measure of the lavers, then, was a cubit and a half, because we are washed in the font of life in that faith that through works of justice we may deserve to enter into life, though we cannot be without sin while we live here; and the very sweetness of the heavenly life we can taste in part and love in this life, but can by no means see it perfectly. The wheels too are measured by a cubit and a half, because the Scripture of the gospel shows how those who would be perfect ought to live, and the hope of eternal recompense, but promises that the very quality of the recompense is to be revealed and given in the future. And the bases had a cubit and a half of breadth at their top, where they received the lavers, because the teachers and ministers of the laver shone in this life, perfect indeed in work, but enjoyed the light of contemplation in part. Whence: "For we know in part, and we prophesy in part" etc.
14_interl1442: that is, on the sides of the bases
14_marg1096: THE SPACES BETWEEN THE PILLARS WERE SQUARE, NOT ROUND etc. He means the upper table, which, like the others, was square and likewise carved, and at its top had a round compass of a cubit and a half, in which the laver was set.
14_marg1097: AFTER THIS MANNER. BEDE. Why ten bases were made and as many lavers set upon them has been said above. But that there was one measure and like carving of all the bases or lavers was not done with this signification, that the merits of all teachers can be equal, but because they have one faith of the gospel by which they are instructed, one sacrament of baptism by which they are washed, one and the same Spirit by which all are consecrated, though they have diverse gifts in that same Spirit, who divides to each as he will.
14_interl1444: in the lavers [they washed] the holocausts, in the sea the priests washed themselves
14_marg1098: ONE LAVER CONTAINED FORTY BATES etc. BEDE. Forty signifies great perfection, because four times ten make forty; and ten are the precepts by which all our working is set beforehand in the law of God, but four the books of the gospels, in which through the dispensation of the Lord's incarnation the entrance of the heavenly homeland has been opened to us. And because all who belong to the mystery of baptism ought, with faith in the sacraments of the gospel, to show the fruit of right working, each of the lavers in which the holocausts were washed held forty bates.
14_marg1099: BEDE. As to what was said above, and together it was one cubit and a half, and he did not add whether it signified breadth or height there, he seems to have wished it understood that the bottom of the laver itself was of this breadth; which is very easily gathered from the measure of the base on which each laver was set, which is described thus: AND IN THE TOP OF THE BASE THERE WAS A ROUND COMPASS OF A CUBIT AND A HALF, SO WROUGHT THAT THE LAVER MIGHT BE SET THEREON. The breadth of the bottom in the lavers, then, was a cubit and a half. But the capacity of the lavers itself had four cubits; but whether he means in height or in breadth or in both, let him say who knows.
14_marg1100: BEDE. On account of the four gospels, in which is the form of baptism; or the cardinal virtues, in which the baptized ought to be instructed; or on account of the four quarters of the world, to which baptism is ministered.
14_marg1101: AND HE SET THE TEN BASES etc. BEDE. But by the right side and left side of the temple he means not within the temple itself, but before the temple toward the eastern quarter, namely in the inner court, which was properly called the priests'. And he placed five on the right side of the temple on account of the Jews, who of old enjoyed the sun of justice through the teaching of the law; and five on the left on account of us, who with blind heart clung for a long time to him who says: "I will place my seat in the north," as if to say: I desire to rest in those hearts which I see to be strangers to the light of truth and the flame of divine charity.
14_marg1102: AND THE SEA HE PUT ON THE RIGHT SIDE etc. BEDE. It too was placed in this same court toward the east. And what he says, on the right side of the temple, is what he repeats saying: southward. For those entering the court from the east had first to turn aside to the south, where the sea stood in the very corner, ready for the priests to wash. Then, as they went on within, the lavers placed on either side met them, for washing the victims. Within these was a brazen base five cubits broad and three cubits high, on which Solomon stood when he dedicated the temple. Then, as they went further on, the altar of holocaust met them, over against the south of the court; then the porch or vestibule of the temple, in which were the brazen columns about the door of the temple. That he placed the sea on the right side of the temple, then, signifies that through the laver of baptism we must come to the heavenly kingdom, which was figured by the right hand: "For he that believeth and is baptized, shall be saved." For where right and left are taken together in a good sense, they designate either Judea and the gentiles, as was said of the bases, or the present life of the Church and the future, or the joys and sorrows of the world, or something of this kind. But where the right is set absolutely in a good sense, it often shows the eternal joys. And that he placed the sea toward the east looks to nearly the same signification, because through the laver of baptism the splendour of inward brightness is opened to us. That [it was] toward the southern side of the court signifies that the faithful, through receiving the Spirit, are kindled to the glow of true charity. For the heat of the noonday sun in the Scriptures signifies the ardour of love and the illumination of the Holy Spirit, through which that same love is poured forth in our hearts.

14_interl1446: brazen vessels of equal breadth at bottom and mouth, for heating
14_marg1103: BEDE. In which the Lord was baptized, and, dipped in its waves, turned the element of waters into the washing of sins for us. And because every baptism of the faithful by which they are consecrated to the Lord is celebrated after the example of that by which he sanctified the waters, rightly were the vessels of the house of the Lord made in the region of the Jordan. For we are not made vessels of election and mercy otherwise than by being busy to be washed in such a river, looking to his baptism. And it is to be noted that he says the same vessels were made not only in the region of the Jordan but in its plain country, signifying the multiplication of the faithful which was to be not only in Judea but in the breadth of all regions, according to that: "The fields and all things that are in them shall be joyful." And elsewhere: "Behold we have heard of it in Ephrata: we have found it in the fields of the wood." For "we have heard in Ephrata," that is, in Bethlehem, the sacraments of the Lord, because we read that it was promised to David, who was of that same city, that Christ would come in the flesh of the fruit of his womb. "We have found them in the fields of the wood," because, revealed in the breadth of the gentiles through the world, we ourselves have known them, seen them, been made partakers. The king, then, cast the vessels of the house of the Lord in the plain country of the Jordan, because Christ will fill the whole breadth of the world with the baptism of salvation, from which he would make vessels of mercy.
14_marg1104: BEDE. [The clay ground,] of which the moulds were made for casting the vessels, is Scripture, from which we take the rule of living well. For as clay hardened by fire shapes vessels, [so] when Scripture shows us the rule of justice which we are to follow, and shows beforehand the examples of the saints, who stood forth invincible in the fire of suffering, to be followed in all things. But we see that the vessels in the house of the Lord are precious, and the brass melted by fire enters the moulds of clay, that a vessel fit for the heavenly ministries may be made, when, wholesomely humbled and softened by the flame of divine charity or of human adversity, we enter the way of the fathers by working well, that by running well we may come to their rewards.
14_marg1105: BEDE. Above he said that Hiram made all the vessels for Solomon; now Scripture adds that Solomon made the same. For Solomon made them by directing, Hiram by working.
14_marg1106: BEDE. [The altar of gold is] the hearts of the perfect, shining with the light of inward charity and chastity. It stood before the door of the Holy of Holies, as is read in the making of the tabernacle, because the saints, neglecting the desires of temporal things, seek heavenly things with their whole intention. They are in the neighbourhood of the oracle, not far from the veil by which the temple and the holy of holies are parted, because in body they dwell on earth, in mind they have their conversation in heaven. From this altar the smoke of the incense goes up within the holy of holies, where the ark is laid up, when the prayers of the saints, stirred up by the flame of charity, reach heaven, where Christ is at the right hand of God. But on this altar not the blood of victims but incense only is burnt, because such men have no works of the flesh to slay to the Lord on the altar of the heart, but offer him only the vows of tears and prayer for desire of the heavenly kingdom.
14_marg1107: BEDE. Moses made the altar of incense "having a cubit of length, and another of breadth, and two in height." But how great was the one Solomon made Scripture does not say. It is certain, however, that it was not so great as that of holocaust, because if it had been made twenty cubits in length and breadth it would have filled the whole breadth of the temple. And yet it was narrower [so the edition: 'angustius'] than the Mosaic, as were all the other things that Solomon made. As much, then, as the altar of holocaust was more outward than that of incense, and as much as it was less noble in kind of offering and cheapness of metal, so much it excelled in size of measure and frequency of victims. Because, no doubt, more delight to hear 'if thou wilt enter into life, keep the commandments' than: "If thou wilt be perfect, go sell what thou hast, and give to the poor." The altar of holocaust holds the type of those who consecrate body and soul to the Lord through the fire of love. Their perseverance in good working is figured by the length of the altar, their breadth in the charity of God and neighbour by the breadth, their hope in the expectation of the divine vision by the height. The books of Moses are five, four [the books] of gospel liberty; and when, the grace of the gospel enlightening us, we come to the spiritual understanding and keeping of the law, we complete four times five, which number is in the length and breadth, when the elect, both Testaments teaching them, keep both the perseverance of good work and the cheerfulness of love. The same altar was ten cubits high, signifying by the denarius the perpetual life of the elect. Whence those who labour in the vineyard of the great householder are rewarded with a denarius.
14_marg1108: BEDE. [The table is] Scripture, bright with spiritual understanding. Of which: "Thou hast prepared a table before me." The loaves of proposition are the holy teachers, whose works or words, set forth to us as an example in the divine pages, he who seeks well finds. Whence the same loaves in Exodus were commanded to be made twelve, on account of the twelve apostles, through whom the Scripture of the new Testament was composed and the mysteries of the old revealed; by whose number all teachers are signified, because they follow that same form of doctrine which the apostles received from the Lord. In the Words of the Days we read that Solomon made "ten tables in the temple, five on the left hand, and five on the right," which, it is to be known, were made for carrying the vessels of the Lord, namely the bowls, which Scripture relates were made at the same time, and the censers in which incense was burned, and the rest. As to what is brought in a little after in the same volume, "Solomon made the tables and upon them the loaves of proposition," either he put the plural for the singular after the manner of Scripture, or surely the newly baked loaves were set on those tables, where they were kept covered that night, until at early morning, the old ones being taken away, they were set hot on the table of proposition. The ten tables do not differ from the figure of the one. For as the one table, laden with twelve loaves, designates the unanimous concord of Scripture, by which we are fed, fortified by apostolic authority, so the ten tables announce the words of the law and the prophets, which set before us the examples of the faithful as the brightness and wonders of the vessels of the Lord set upon them. The tables are twice five: five, because the law embraces both five books and five ages of the world; twice, because after the Lord's incarnation it is committed to both peoples, namely Jew and gentile, and because it is shown to be full of figures, which once was thought to be understood according to the letter.
14_marg1109: BEDE. As the tables are put in type of Scripture, because they minister the bread of the word and bear the vessels of ministry, that is, set before us the acts of the just as an example, so the same is figured by the candlesticks, because it brings forth the light of wisdom to the erring. Whence Solomon: "The commandment is a lamp, and the law a light." That the candlesticks were five on the right and five on the left is the same as was said above of the tables. The oracle where the ark was is the entrance of the heavenly homeland, where Christ sits at the right hand of God, privy indeed to the Father's secrets. The candlesticks are over against the oracle, because the words of God look toward the dwelling of the city above, to kindle us to deserve it. The lamps are holy men, who, infused with the oil of the Holy Spirit, both burn themselves with the fire of love in the heart and hold out to their neighbours the light of knowledge on the tongue. The candlesticks, which lift the lamps on high, are sacred Scripture, which shows the virtues and doctrine of the saints by its reading. Whence it is said of John: "He was a burning and a shining light." Or else the lamps are the divine words. Whence: "Thy word is a lamp to my feet." The candlesticks of the lamps are the saints, who put their hearts and bodies under to carry the commandments of the Lord. For whoever cares to follow his own will in nothing, but attends to what Scripture says, and is busy to submit himself to its commands and to hearken to its promises, bears golden lamps as a golden candlestick, and this with as fixed an intention as the candlestick, set upright toward the heights, keeps the lamps set on it without moving. The lily flowers designate the pleasantness of the ever-green land of the living. Well are these flowers on the candlestick, because Scripture is wont to call us to seek heavenly things, earthly things being despised; and as the upright candlestick has lamps and lily flowers on its head, so the elect who are contained in Scripture, with sense raised up to the heights, seek and receive heavenly goods from the Lord.
14_marg1110: BEDE. This seems to say that the top part of the candlesticks was shaped in the manner of a crisped lily. By the lamps of gold over them, that which contains being put for what is contained, are designated the little golden vessels in which the oil gave light.
14_marg1111: BEDE. That is, the snuffers with which the wicks were snuffed, that, renewed, they might give better light.
14_marg1112: The pots signify the hearts of the saints, filled with the water of wisdom and the wine of compunction.
14_marg1113: The fleshhooks, with which the meats are prepared, are the preachers, who minister to their hearers the food of understanding, whose office is to distribute the body and blood to believers and to deny it to unbelievers.
14_interl1450: the labour of penance and the suffering of endurance, by which their members upon the earth are mortified
14_interl1451: the virtues of works or the prayers of the saints, by which the odour of sweetness goes up to God from a pure conscience and faith unfeigned
14_marg1114: BEDE. The doors of the inner house are the angelic ministries, which unbar for us, when we have gone forth from the body, the entrance of the heavenly life. The doors of the house of the temple are the teachers and priests, who by instructing, baptizing, and communicating the mysteries of the Lord's body and blood, open to us the first thresholds of the present Church. The hinges of both doors are the senses and hearts of angels and saints, by which they cling immovably to the contemplation and love of the creator, that they may rightly fulfil the ministry delegated to them in that they never turn their eyes from the will of the Lord. For the doors are opened and shut, but do not leave the hinge, because angels and saints, whether they receive the faithful and elect in this life of faith or in that of sight, always keep their mind fixed in the root of inward love. Whence well were the hinges made of gold, on account of faith, or the merit of their own brightness, or of the charity which they have toward God.
14_marg1115: HE FINISHED ALL THE WORK etc. BEDE. While the state of the world goes on, [Solomon] makes indeed the work of the house of the Lord but does not yet finish it, because the Lord inspires and helps the hearts of the elect to work good things, yet grants to none dwelling in this life to be without sin; for he reserves this for the future beatitude. But he finishes all the work of the temple of Solomon and makes it fit for dedication when our peacemaker on the last day glorifies the elect with the immortality of the resurrection and leads them to the eternal kingdom. Whence the temple, built in seven years, was finished and dedicated in the eighth. To which time fits what follows: AND BROUGHT IN THE THINGS THAT [DAVID] HAD DEDICATED etc. David, the father of Solomon, had sanctified the silver when God the Father strengthens the eloquent by the grace of his Spirit to speak the word of God. He sanctifies the gold when he enlightens those endowed with natural wit to understand the law. He sanctifies the vessels too when he bestows the grace of the Holy Spirit on all the sons of the Church. These sanctified things Solomon brings into the temple when the Lord, the judgment being finished, brings the company of teachers and the other faithful into the joy of the heavenly kingdom. AND LAID THEM UP IN THE TREASURES OF THE HOUSE OF THE LORD, because God hides his own in the secret of his face from the disturbance of men. There are many treasures in the one house of the Lord, because in the one Church the saints differ in merits. And there is one heavenly homeland, though in it star differs from star in glory. Both of which the distributor of rewards showed when he said: "In my Father's house there are many mansions."
